sections.heading: Evolution & historical background of the Constitution

blocks.text: The Indian Constitution evolved from a **series of British colonial Acts (1773–1947)** and the **Constituent Assembly (1946–49)**. It draws on this legislative inheritance and world constitutions, and was **adopted on 26 Nov 1949** and **enforced on 26 Jan 1950**.

rows: First steps of Crown control over the Company.
Crown rule; **Indians in legislatures; separate electorates (1909)**.
**Dyarchy (1919); provincial autonomy, federation (1935)** — the biggest source of the Constitution.
Formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan**; **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** President; **Ambedkar** chaired Drafting Committee; took **2 yrs 11 mo 18 days**.

items: GoI Act 1935 = biggest single source; Constituent Assembly under Cabinet Mission (1946).
Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950; took 2 yrs 11 months 18 days.

prelimsPointers: **GoI Act 1935** is the **largest single source** of the Constitution.
**Separate electorates** introduced by the **Morley-Minto Act (1909)**.
Constituent Assembly formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**; first met **9 Dec 1946**.
**Dr. Rajendra Prasad** — President of the Assembly; **B.R. Ambedkar** — Chairman, Drafting Committee.
**B.N. Rau** — Constitutional Advisor; **objective resolution** moved by **Nehru**.
Constitution **adopted 26 Nov 1949 (Constitution Day)**; **came into force 26 Jan 1950**.
Took **2 years, 11 months, 18 days** to frame.
mainsAngles: Trace the historical evolution of the Indian Constitution.

glossary.definition: The body (1946-49) that framed the Indian Constitution under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
The colonial act that is the single largest source of provisions in the Indian Constitution.
26 November, marking the adoption of the Constitution in 1949.

blocks.text: The Indian Constitution is the **world's lengthiest written constitution**, blending features borrowed from many nations. Its **Preamble** — the 'soul' and 'identity card' — declares India a **Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic** committed to Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

rows: Longest written constitution; a blend of **rigid & flexible**.
**Parliamentary govt & rule of law (UK), FR & judicial review (USA), DPSP (Ireland), emergency (Germany), Concurrent list (Australia), FD & planning (USSR)**.
**Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic**; Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
Added **'Socialist, Secular, Integrity'** to the Preamble.
Part of the Constitution (Kesavananda); reflects its **basic structure**.

items: Borrowings by country (UK-parliamentary, USA-FR, Ireland-DPSP, USSR-FD) is a top MCQ.
42nd Amendment (1976) added Socialist/Secular/Integrity to the Preamble.

prelimsPointers: India has the **world's lengthiest written constitution**.

Borrowings — **UK (parliamentary govt, rule of law, single citizenship), USA (Fundamental Rights, judicial review, preamble), Ireland (DPSP), Canada (federation with strong centre), Australia (Concurrent list), USSR (Fundamental Duties)**.
**Preamble** describes India as **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** added **'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity'**.
**Preamble is part of the Constitution** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) and is amendable.
'**We, the People of India**' — source of authority is the people.
The Preamble is based on the **Objectives Resolution** (Nehru).
mainsAngles: Discuss the significance of the Preamble and the salient features of the Constitution.

glossary.definition: The introductory statement of the Constitution declaring its ideals and source of authority.
A state with no official religion, treating all faiths equally; added to the Preamble in 1976.
The core constitutional principles that cannot be amended away (Kesavananda Bharati case).

blocks.text: **Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12–35)** are the **justiciable guarantees** protecting citizens against state action, enforceable through the **Supreme Court (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226)**. They are the 'Magna Carta' of the Constitution.

rows: **Arts. 14-18** (equality before law, no discrimination, abolition of untouchability & titles).
**Arts. 19-22** (speech, assembly, movement; protection in arrest — Art. 21 life & liberty).
**Art. 32** — Ambedkar's 'heart and soul'; writs — habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto.

items: Six FRs; Art. 32 = 'heart and soul' (Ambedkar); Art. 21 broadened hugely by the judiciary.
Right to Property was removed as an FR by the 44th Amendment (now Art. 300A, legal right).

prelimsPointers: Fundamental Rights — **Part III, Articles 12-35**; originally **7, now 6** (property removed).
**Right to Equality (14-18); Right to Freedom (19-22); Against Exploitation (23-24); Freedom of Religion (25-28); Cultural & Educational (29-30); Constitutional Remedies (32)**.
**Article 32** — 'heart and soul of the Constitution' (Ambedkar); provides **five writs**.
**Article 21** (life & personal liberty) — expanded to include privacy, environment, education etc.
**Article 21A** — Right to Education (6-14 yrs), added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
**Right to Property** removed as FR by the **44th Amendment (1978)** → **Article 300A** (legal right).
FRs are **justiciable** and can be **suspended during a National Emergency** (except 20 & 21).
mainsAngles: Examine the scope and significance of Fundamental Rights.

glossary.definition: Justiciable rights in Part III that protect individuals against arbitrary state action.
A judicial order (habeas corpus, mandamus, etc.) issued to enforce Fundamental Rights under Arts. 32/226.
The right to constitutional remedies, called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

blocks.text: **Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A)** are the **moral obligations of citizens**, added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**, inspired by the **USSR** Constitution. Originally 10, now **11**.

rows: **Swaran Singh Committee**; inspired by the **USSR** Constitution.
Originally **10**; the **11th** (education of child 6-14) added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
Respect the Constitution, flag & anthem; protect environment; promote harmony; safeguard public property.

items: 42nd Amendment (1976), Swaran Singh Committee, USSR inspiration; Part IVA / Art 51A.
Now 11 duties (11th added by 86th Amendment 2002); non-justiciable.

prelimsPointers: **Fundamental Duties** — **Part IVA, Article 51A**; added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
Recommended by the **Swaran Singh Committee**; inspired by the **USSR (erstwhile) Constitution**.
Originally **10 duties**; the **11th** (parent to provide education, 6-14 yrs) added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
Fundamental Duties are **non-justiciable** (no legal enforcement).
Apply only to **citizens** (not foreigners).
Examples — respect the **National Flag & Anthem**, protect the **environment**, develop **scientific temper**.
India is one of the few countries to list citizens' duties in its constitution.
mainsAngles: Discuss the significance and limitations of Fundamental Duties.

glossary.definition: Non-justiciable moral obligations of citizens in Part IVA (Art. 51A).
The 1976 committee that recommended adding Fundamental Duties to the Constitution.
The 1976 'mini-constitution' amendment that inserted Fundamental Duties and Preamble words.

blocks.text: **Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36–51)** are **non-justiciable guidelines** directing the state to secure a **welfare state and social-economic justice**. Borrowed from **Ireland**, they are 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.

rows: Equal pay, living wage, right to work, public health (Arts. 38, 39, 41, 43).
Village panchayats (40), cottage industries, prohibition (47), cow protection (48), SC/ST welfare (46).
**Uniform Civil Code (44)**, separation of judiciary from executive (50), environment & wildlife (48A), international peace (51).
**FR vs DPSP** — resolved via harmony (Minerva Mills: balance is basic structure).

items: DPSP = Part IV, borrowed from Ireland, non-justiciable; classified socialistic/Gandhian/liberal.
UCC (Art 44), Panchayats (40), environment (48A) are frequently asked.

prelimsPointers: **DPSP** — **Part IV, Articles 36-51**; borrowed from the **Irish Constitution**.
**Non-justiciable** but **'fundamental in the governance of the country'**.
Classified — **Socialistic, Gandhian, Liberal-intellectual**.
**Article 40** — organisation of **village panchayats**; **Article 44** — **Uniform Civil Code**.
**Article 48A** (environment) & **Article 51A(g)** (duty) added by **42nd Amendment**.
**Article 50** — separation of judiciary from executive.
In **FR vs DPSP** conflict, courts seek **harmony** (Minerva Mills — balance = basic structure).
mainsAngles: Examine the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

glossary.definition: Directive Principles — non-justiciable guidelines (Part IV) directing the state towards a welfare state.
The directive (Art. 44) for a common civil law for all citizens regardless of religion.
A state that promotes social and economic well-being, the goal of the DPSPs.
